metadata.title: TRUST AT SCALE: THE ECONOMIC LIMITS OF CRYPTOCURRENCIES AND BLOCKCHAINS

raw_text.abstract: Satoshi Nakamoto (2008) invented a new kind of economic system that can record and verify transactions without reliance on any trusted intermediary such as a bank, government, or rule of law. Trust and security instead arise from a combination of cryptography, peer-to-peer networking, and a proof-of-work consensus mechanism. In this article, I study whether this technology can scale to support a large quantity of economic activity at low or zero marginal cost.
raw_text.keywords_text: cryptocurrencies, blockchains, consensus security, majority attacks, proof-of-work, transaction fees

theoretical_summary: Economic security constraints imply that permissionless blockchains cannot scale to support large volumes of activity without either very high costs or reliance on external enforcement mechanisms.

metadata.title: WAR REPARATIONS, STRUCTURAL CHANGE, AND INTERGENERATIONAL MOBILITY

raw_text.abstract: From 1944 to 1952, largely agrarian Finland had to export, on a large scale, industrial products to the Soviet Union as war reparations. To meet the reparation demands, Finland launched a nationwide industrial policy that expanded manufacturing and reshaped local economies. This article documents long-run effects on industrial development and intergenerational outcomes, finding that more exposed regions became persistently more industrialized and experienced improved mobility.
raw_text.keywords_text: war reparations, industrial policy, structural change, manufacturing, regional development, intergenerational mobility, Finland

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: adult taxable earnings (or earnings rank) from linked administrative records of cohorts
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: region’s pre-reparations employment share in industries producing war reparations (exposure index) interacted with reparations-driven demand
empirical_analysis.methodology: difference-in-differences comparing more- vs less-exposed Finnish regions before and after the 1944–1952 reparations period
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: triple-difference using comparable Norwegian industry-region data; alternative exposure measures; pre-trend checks
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Finland wartime reparations episode (1944–1952); newly digitized industry/region production and employment data (roughly 1934–1970) linked to administrative microdata tracking individuals into adulthood
empirical_analysis.control_variables: region and cohort fixed effects; baseline industry structure; pre-war trends; demographics
subject: Estimate how exposure to Finland’s WWII war-reparations industrial policy affected structural change and intergenerational mobility.

metadata.title: A WELFARE ANALYSIS OF TAX AUDITS ACROSS THE INCOME DISTRIBUTION

raw_text.abstract: We estimate the returns to IRS audits of taxpayers across the income distribution and compare the welfare costs of raising revenue through audits at different income levels. We find that an additional $1 spent auditing taxpayers above the 90th income percentile yields substantially higher revenue than auditing lower-income taxpayers, and we incorporate distributional welfare weights to assess the social costs of audit-based revenue collection.
raw_text.keywords_text: tax audits, tax compliance, tax revenue, income distribution, welfare costs, Internal Revenue Service

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: additional tax revenue attributable to audits (direct collections plus subsequent payments) net of audit resource costs
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: audit intensity by income group measured via marginal audit spending / audit probability across the income distribution
empirical_analysis.methodology: administrative-data estimation of audit returns by income group combined with a welfare calculation using marginal utility of income to compare welfare costs per dollar raised
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: alternative audit-cost and compliance assumptions; checks using randomly selected audits as benchmarks; alternative revenue horizons
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: U.S. IRS administrative tax return and audit data for tax years 2010–2014, including subsequent compliance and payment outcomes
empirical_analysis.control_variables: income and filing characteristics; return type; claim indicators (e.g., credits); year effects
subject: Quantify how the fiscal and welfare returns to IRS tax audits vary across the income distribution.

metadata.title: MEASURING AND MITIGATING RACIAL DISPARITIES IN TAX AUDITS

raw_text.abstract: We study differences in Internal Revenue Service audit rates between Black and non-Black taxpayers. Because neither we nor the IRS observe taxpayer race, we propose methods to estimate disparities when race is unobserved and evaluate how audit targeting policies contribute to observed gaps. We analyze audit selection and outcomes, highlighting the role of refundable credit enforcement and considering policy changes that could reduce disparities.
raw_text.keywords_text: racial disparities, tax audits, refundable credits, Earned Income Tax Credit, tax compliance, Internal Revenue Service

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: probability a tax return is audited (and audit type), measured in IRS administrative records
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: probabilistic race assignment using Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding (BISG) from surname and geography
empirical_analysis.methodology: analysis of IRS audit selection and outcomes with partial-identification methods to estimate disparities when true race is unobserved; counterfactual policy simulations of audit targeting
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: alternative race-imputation specifications; sensitivity bounds; subgroup analyses by credit claiming and income
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: U.S. IRS administrative audit and return data centered on tax year 2014 (and adjacent years referenced in the paper)
empirical_analysis.control_variables: income; filing status; refundable credit claims; return characteristics; geography
subject: Measure racial disparities in IRS audit selection and evaluate policy changes that could reduce those disparities.

metadata.title: THE GLOBAL RACE FOR TALENT: BRAIN DRAIN, KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER, AND GROWTH

raw_text.abstract: I build a novel two-country innovation-led endogenous growth framework to study how inventors’ migration affects international innovation, knowledge transfer, and long-run growth. The analysis links inventor movements to changes in innovative output and spillovers across countries, documenting how migration reshapes the geography of innovation and the distribution of gains between origin and destination economies.
raw_text.keywords_text: brain drain, inventor migration, innovation, knowledge transfer, patents, H-1B visas, economic growth

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: inventor-level patent output (counts and/or quality proxies such as citations) from U.S. and EU patent records
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: inventor cross-border moves inferred from changes in inventor location across patent filings (U.S.–EU corridor)
empirical_analysis.methodology: event-study and difference-in-differences estimates of inventor productivity around migration, combined with a two-country innovation-and-growth model calibrated to match observed facts
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: pre-trend/event-time placebo checks; alternative migration definitions; analyses by field and origin/destination
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Inventor-level U.S. and EU patent data with migration measurement (illustrative window shown as 2000–2010 in the paper)
empirical_analysis.control_variables: inventor experience; technology field; origin/destination fixed effects; time effects
subject: Assess how inventor migration shapes international innovation, knowledge transfer, and long-run growth.

metadata.title: RESERVES WERE NOT SO AMPLE AFTER ALL

raw_text.abstract: We show that the likelihood of a liquidity crunch in dollar funding markets depends on levels of reserve balances at the financial institutions that are the most active intermediaries. As reserves declined, repo rates became more sensitive to the distribution of reserves and to intraday payment timing, helping explain stress episodes such as the September 2019 spike in repo rates.
raw_text.keywords_text: bank reserves, repo markets, liquidity, SOFR, intraday payments, Federal Reserve, money markets

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: money-market stress proxied by repo rates and spreads such as SOFR minus the interest on reserves (IOR)
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: reserve balances at the most repo-active financial institutions from Federal Reserve account data
empirical_analysis.methodology: empirical analysis linking reserve distribution and intraday payment timing to spikes in repo rates and liquidity stress (including episodes like September 2019)
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: alternative stress measures (other repo rates/spreads); quantile-based specifications; alternative sample windows around stress episodes
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: U.S. reserve and funding-market data including Fed account reserve balances, repo rates, and intraday payment measures, focused on 2018–2019 with related stress-episode analysis
empirical_analysis.control_variables: market conditions (rates/volatility); institution characteristics; day and time fixed effects
subject: Explain how reserve distribution and payment timing affected liquidity stress and repo-rate spikes when reserves declined.

metadata.title: LINKEDOUT? A FIELD EXPERIMENT ON DISCRIMINATION IN JOB NETWORK FORMATION

raw_text.abstract: We assess the impact of discrimination on Black individuals’ job networks across the United States using a two-stage field experiment with 400+ fictitious LinkedIn profiles. In the first stage, profiles send connection requests and measure acceptance; in the second stage, accepted connections receive follow-up interactions to test downstream treatment. The results indicate substantial gatekeeping and suggest that discrimination in network formation is a key driver of Black–white disparities.
raw_text.keywords_text: labor markets, job networks, discrimination, LinkedIn, social capital, Black workers

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: LinkedIn connection-request acceptance rate and subsequent response/engagement in the experiment
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: race signaled on fictitious LinkedIn profiles via an AI-based race-varying profile algorithm (name/photo cues)
empirical_analysis.methodology: two-stage field experiment on LinkedIn using fictitious profiles to measure discrimination in network formation and downstream interactions
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: varying profile attributes and contexts; placebo checks on non-network outcomes; heterogeneity across target-user characteristics
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: U.S. LinkedIn field experiment with 400+ fictitious profiles and ~20,000 targeted users (study period around early-2020s as described in the paper)
empirical_analysis.control_variables: profile qualifications; target-user industry/region; timing controls
subject: Test whether discrimination reduces Black individuals’ job-network formation and identify mechanisms behind network disparities.

metadata.title: OVERINFERENCE FROM WEAK SIGNALS AND UNDERINFERENCE FROM STRONG SIGNALS

raw_text.abstract: We show that a key driver of whether people overinfer or underinfer is the strength of the information. Based on a model in which people know which direction information points but misperceive its strength, we reconcile contradictory results across experimental and empirical settings using evidence from belief-updating experiments, sports prediction markets, and financial-market data.
raw_text.keywords_text: belief updating, information strength, prediction markets, sports betting, options markets, miscalibration

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: deviation of belief revisions from Bayesian updating (posterior changes) in experiments and market-implied probability revisions
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: signal strength measured by objective informativeness (likelihood ratio / forecastability) of the underlying signal in each setting
empirical_analysis.methodology: behavioral model of belief updating tested with lab/online experiments, prediction-market transactions, and financial-market data
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: replication across multiple environments (experiments, sports prediction markets, options markets); alternative signal-strength constructions; subgroup analyses
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Experimental belief-updating data plus market data including >5 million sports prediction-market transactions and long-run S&P 500 options price data (multi-decade)
empirical_analysis.control_variables: prior beliefs; event characteristics; participant demographics (in experiments); time controls
subject: Explain why people overreact to weak information and underreact to strong information across experimental and real-world settings.

metadata.title: BELIEVED GENDER DIFFERENCES IN SOCIAL PREFERENCES

raw_text.abstract: While there is a vast (and mixed) literature on gender differences in social preferences, much less is known about believed gender differences in social preferences. Using data from 15 studies and 8,979 participants, we document systematic beliefs about how men and women differ in altruism, fairness, and trust, and we discuss how these beliefs relate to policy preferences and distributional implications.
raw_text.keywords_text: gender beliefs, social preferences, altruism, fairness, trust, stereotypes, policy attitudes

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: elicited beliefs about men’s vs women’s social preferences using survey/experimental belief elicitation across studies
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: indicator for the target gender (male vs female) whose preferences are being evaluated in belief-elicitation tasks
empirical_analysis.methodology: analysis of pooled evidence from 15 studies combining surveys and experiments, comparing believed gender gaps to measured preference gaps
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: study-by-study consistency checks; controls for participant demographics; comparisons across preference domains and contexts
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Compilation of 15 survey/experimental studies covering 8,979 participants (multi-study dataset reported in the paper)
empirical_analysis.control_variables: participant gender and demographics; study fixed effects; context indicators
subject: Measure believed gender differences in social preferences and relate those beliefs to policy and distributional implications.

metadata.title: THE LONG-RUN IMPACTS OF PUBLIC INDUSTRIAL INVESTMENT ON LOCAL DEVELOPMENT AND ECONOMIC MOBILITY: EVIDENCE FROM WORLD WAR II

raw_text.abstract: This article studies the long-run effects of government-led construction of manufacturing plants on the regions where they were built and on individuals from those regions. Specifically, it examines publicly financed WWII plants sited in dispersed locations for security reasons and links these investments to persistent changes in local employment, development, and later-life earnings and mobility for children who grew up in affected counties.
raw_text.keywords_text: public investment, manufacturing plants, World War II, local development, economic mobility, county outcomes, United States

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: adult earnings from longitudinally linked administrative and survey data for individuals from affected counties
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: county exposure to publicly financed WWII manufacturing-plant construction (presence/intensity of plant construction)
empirical_analysis.methodology: quasi-experimental difference-in-differences/event-study comparing counties that received WWII plants (sited for security) to similar counties that did not
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: matched-county comparisons; placebo timing tests; alternative exposure definitions and weighting schemes
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: U.S. WWII publicly financed plant construction records (1940s) linked to longitudinal administrative and survey microdata tracking individuals into adulthood (outcomes observed through late-20th/early-21st century)
empirical_analysis.control_variables: pre-war county characteristics; cohort effects; demographics; baseline industrial structure
subject: Estimate the long-run effects of WWII-era public manufacturing investment on local development and intergenerational economic mobility.

metadata.title: Mandatory Notice of Layoff, Job Search, and Efficiency

raw_text.abstract: In all OECD countries, mandatory notice (MN) policies require firms to inform workers in advance of a layoff. In our theoretical framework, MN helps workers avoid unemployment and find better jobs by encouraging them to search for a new job while still employed, thereby increasing future production. The magnitude of this production gain depends on the relative effectiveness of search while employed versus unemployed. But on-the-job search and diminished work incentives reduce current production. If future gains outweigh current production losses, longer advance notice improves production efficiency. If not, Coasian bargaining predicts that firms offer a larger severance instead of longer notice. With bargaining, the sole efficiency loss of MN is due to delayed separations of unproductive job matches. We test these predictions using novel Swedish administrative data on layoff notifications. Workers eligible for extended MN receive longer notice and larger severance, resulting in less exposure to nonemployment spells and higher-paying jobs. These favorable labor market outcomes are solely due to longer notice; in contrast, larger severance delays job finding and has no impact on wages. We also show that advance notice replaces job search while unemployed with more effective search while employed. On the production side, we document a productivity drop among notified workers and estimate a production loss due to delayed separations. Using our estimates of production gains and losses to evaluate the overall production efficiency, we conclude that the gains of MN seem to outweigh the losses. JEL codes: J24, J63, J65.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: post-notification annual labor earnings and reemployment wages from Swedish matched employer–employee administrative records; nonemployment measured as months without employment/unemployment insurance spells
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: advance notice length (months) measured as displacement date minus notification date, with exogenous variation from age-55 eligibility for extended mandatory notice in collective bargaining agreements
empirical_analysis.methodology: quasi-experimental estimates exploiting the age-55 threshold for extended mandatory notice and an additional instrument based on the share of laid-off coworkers above 55 to separate notice from severance effects, combined with firm-side output measures to quantify production gains and losses
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: covariate balance and manipulation tests around the age cutoff; alternative bandwidths and polynomial orders; placebo thresholds; sensitivity to excluding bankruptcies and alternative outcome windows
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Sweden 2005–2016: Public Employment Service layoff-notification records linked to matched employer–employee administrative data, unemployment-spell registers, wage survey data, and firm financial accounts
empirical_analysis.control_variables: worker demographics (age, gender, education, immigrant status), baseline earnings, tenure, month-by-year effects, firm and layoff-event characteristics, and industry controls
subject: Estimate how longer mandatory layoff notice affects job search timing, nonemployment exposure, post-layoff earnings, and production efficiency.

metadata.title: Do Financial Concerns Make Workers Less Productive?

raw_text.abstract: Workers who are worried about their personal finances may find it hard to focus at work. If so, reducing financial concerns could increase productivity. We test this hypothesis in a sample of low-income Indian piece-rate manufacturing workers. We stagger when wages are paid out: some workers are paid earlier and receive a cash infusion while others remain liquidity constrained. The cash infusion leads workers to reduce their financial concerns by immediately paying off debts and buying household essentials. Subsequently, they become more productive at work: their output increases by 7% (0.11 std. dev.), and they make fewer costly, unintentional mistakes. JEL codes: D91, J24, J28, O15.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: daily piece-rate output (plates produced per shift) and unintentional mistake rate from production records, standardized within experimental rounds
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: indicator for receiving an early wage payout that provides a cash infusion versus receiving the payout later in the pay cycle (staggered payroll timing assignment)
empirical_analysis.methodology: staggered wage-payment experiment among piece-rate manufacturing workers, comparing post-payment productivity when workers receive early versus delayed wages while holding work conditions constant across rounds
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: placebo and pre-treatment day checks; alternative productivity measures (output vs quality); controls for attendance, fatigue, and learning; heterogeneity by baseline debt and financial strain
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Rural Odisha, India (March–June 2017–2018): 14 experimental rounds with 408 low-income male workers employed for two-week contract jobs making disposable plates; linked surveys on debt and financial strain plus production records
empirical_analysis.control_variables: worker characteristics and baseline financial conditions, round and day effects, task conditions, and baseline productivity controls
subject: Test whether reducing workers’ financial concerns through short-term liquidity infusions increases on-the-job productivity and reduces mistakes.

metadata.title: Present Bias Amplifies the Household Balance-Sheet Channels of Macroeconomic Policy

raw_text.abstract: We study the effect of monetary and fiscal policy in a heterogeneous-agent model where households have present-biased time preferences and naive beliefs. The model features a liquid asset and illiquid home equity, which households can use as collateral for borrowing. Because present bias substantially increases households’ marginal propensity to consume (MPC), present bias increases the effect of fiscal policy. Present bias also amplifies the effect of monetary policy, but at the same time, slows down the speed of monetary transmission. Interest rate cuts incentivize households to conduct cash-out refinances, which become targeted liquidity injections to high-MPC households. Present bias also introduces a motive for households to procrastinate refinancing their mortgages, which slows down the speed with which this monetary channel operates. JEL codes: E21, E60, G51.

theoretical_summary: In a heterogeneous-agent model with present-biased, naive households and liquid/illiquid balance sheets, present bias raises MPCs and amplifies fiscal and monetary policy effects while slowing monetary transmission through refinance procrastination.

metadata.title: A Cognitive View of Policing

raw_text.abstract: What causes adverse policing outcomes, such as excessive uses of force and unnecessary arrests? Prevailing explanations focus on problematic officers or deficient regulations and oversight. We introduce an overlooked perspective. We suggest that the cognitive demands inherent in policing can undermine officer decision making. Unless officers are prepared for these demands, they may jump to conclusions too quickly without fully considering alternative ways of seeing a situation. This can lead to adverse policing outcomes. To test this perspective, we created a new training that teaches officers to consider different ways of interpreting the situations they encounter. We evaluated this training using a randomized controlled trial with 2,070 officers from the Chicago Police Department. In a series of lab assessments, we find that treated officers were significantly more likely to consider a wider range of evidence and develop more explanations for subjects’ actions. Critically, we also find that training affected officer performance in the field, leading to reductions in uses of force, discretionary arrests, and arrests of Black civilians. Meanwhile, officer activity levels remained unchanged, and trained officers were less likely to be injured on duty. Our results highlight the value of considering the cognitive aspects of policing and demonstrate the power of using behaviorally informed approaches to improve officer decision making and policing outcomes. JEL codes: C91, C93, D91, K42, M53.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: uses-of-force incidents per officer from Chicago Police Department administrative records
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: indicator for assignment to the Sit-D (See It Differently) cognitive decision-making training
empirical_analysis.methodology: randomized controlled trial evaluating behaviorally informed police training
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: balance checks, alternative specifications, attrition and spillover tests
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Chicago Police Department, 2020–2021
empirical_analysis.control_variables: officer characteristics, pre-treatment outcomes, district and time controls
subject: Evaluate whether a cognitive decision-making training for police officers reduces adverse policing outcomes.

metadata.title: Costs of Financing U.S. Federal Debt under a Gold Standard: 1791–1933

raw_text.abstract: From a new data set, we infer time series of term structures of yields on U.S. federal bonds during the gold standard era from 1791–1933 and use our estimates to reassess historical narratives about how the United States expanded its fiscal capacity.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: estimated zero-coupon yield curves from historical bond prices
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: policy regime indicators and historical episode timing
empirical_analysis.methodology: historical yield curve reconstruction and risk-premium decomposition
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: alternative bond samples and pricing assumptions
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: U.S. federal bonds, 1791–1933
empirical_analysis.control_variables: bond characteristics and liquidity proxies
subject: Assess how gold-standard institutions affected U.S. federal debt financing costs.

metadata.title: WHEN DID GROWTH BEGIN? NEW ESTIMATES OF PRODUCTIVITY GROWTH IN ENGLAND FROM 1250 TO 1870

raw_text.abstract: We estimate productivity growth in England from 1250 to 1870. Real wages over this period were heavily inﬂuenced by plague-induced swings in the population. Our estimates account for these Malthusian dynamics. We ﬁnd that productivity growth was zero before 1600. Productivity growth began in 1600—almost a century before the Glorious Revolution. Thus, the onset of productivity growth preceded the bourgeois institutional reforms of seventeenth-century England. We estimate productivity growth of 2% per decade between 1600 and 1800, increasing to 5% per decade between 1810 and 1860. Much of the increase in output growth during the Industrial Revolution is explained by structural change—the falling importance of land in production—rather than faster productivity growth. Stagnant real wages in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries—Engels’ Pause—is explained by rapid population growth putting downward pressure on real wages. Yet feedback from population growth to real wages is sufﬁciently weak to permit sustained deviations from the “iron law of wages” prior to the Industrial Revolution.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: real daily wage index for unskilled building workers (Clark 2010), converted to decadal averages and log real wages
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: England population estimates (Clark 2007b population-trend series pre-1540; Wrigley et al. 1997 post-1540), decadal averages and log labor supply proxy
empirical_analysis.methodology: Estimate the slope of labor demand using the Black Death population shock and structurally estimate a Malthusian model linking wages and population; infer productivity as shifts in the labor-demand curve (and a Malmquist productivity index with time-varying factor elasticities after 1760) and estimate structural breaks in long-run productivity growth.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Alternative wage series (farmers/craftsmen; alternative historical wage reconstructions); alternative population series and measurement-error assumptions; alternative break-date windows; models incorporating capital accumulation and allowing land’s output elasticity to fall using land-rent data.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: England, decadal series from 1250–1870 using historical real-wage series (Clark 2010), population series (Clark 2007b; Wrigley et al. 1997), and post-1760 land-rent information to pin down changing factor shares.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: land treated as fixed factor in baseline; post-1760 calibration uses land rents and allows time-varying factor elasticities; model-implied population dynamics net out plague-driven labor-supply shocks
subject: Estimate when sustained productivity growth began in England by separating Malthusian population-driven wage movements from underlying productivity shifts.

metadata.title: GENERATIVE AI AT WORK

raw_text.abstract: We study the staggered introduction of a generative AI–based conversational assistant using data from 5,172 customer-support agents. Access to AI assistance increases worker productivity, as measured by issues resolved per hour, by 15% on average, with substantial heterogeneity across workers. The effects vary signiﬁcantly across different agents. Less experienced and lower-skilled workers improve both the speed and quality of their output, while the most experienced and highest-skilled workers see small gains in speed and small declines in quality. We also ﬁnd evidence that AI assistance facilitates worker learning and improves English ﬂuency, particularly among international agents. While AI systems improve with more training data, we ﬁnd that the gains from AI adoption are largest for moderately rare problems, where human agents have less baseline experience but the system still has adequate training data. Finally, we provide evidence that AI assistance improves the experience of work along several dimensions: customers are more polite and less likely to ask to speak to a manager.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: issues resolved per hour (resolutions per hour) computed from platform records; components include average handle time, chats per hour, and resolution rate aggregated to agent-month
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: indicator for whether a customer-support agent has access to the GPT-3–based conversational assistant in a given month based on staggered rollout and training completion
empirical_analysis.methodology: Compare agents before vs after AI-tool access with agent and month fixed effects, exploiting staggered individual onboarding; quantify heterogeneous effects by baseline skill/tenure and topic rarity and examine mechanisms using text features and unplanned tool outages.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Event-time patterns around onboarding; team-level adoption instrument checks; placebo timing tests; sensitivity to tenure controls and alternative productivity components; analyses exploiting unexpected outages to test persistence (learning) of effects.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Fortune 500 business-process software firm’s chat-based customer support, ~3 million chats from 5,172 agents, with staggered AI rollout mainly during fall 2020–winter 2021; outcomes constructed from internal performance systems and chat text.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: agent fixed effects; year-month fixed effects; tenure-in-months controls; (where available) employer/subcontractor and team controls
subject: Measure how a generative-AI chat assistant changes customer-support agents’ productivity, quality, learning, and customer interactions in real workplace use.

metadata.title: COGNITIVE ENDURANCE AS HUMAN CAPITAL

raw_text.abstract: Schooling may build human capital not only by teaching academic skills but by expanding the capacity for cognition. We focus speciﬁcally on cognitive endurance: the ability to sustain effortful mental activity over a continuous stretch of time. As motivation, we document that globally and in the United States, the poor exhibit cognitive fatigue more quickly than the rich do across ﬁeld settings; they also attend schools that offer fewer opportunities to practice thinking for continuous stretches. Using a ﬁeld experiment with 1,600 Indian primary school students, we randomly increase the amount of time students spend in sustained cognitive activity during the school day—using either math problems (mimicking good schooling) or nonacademic games (providing a pure test of our mechanism). Each approach markedly improves cognitive endurance: students show 22% less decline in performance over time when engaged in intellectual activities—listening comprehension, academic problems, or IQ tests. They also exhibit increased attentiveness in the classroom and score higher on psychological measures of sustained attention. Moreover, each treatment improves students’ school performance by 0.09 standard deviations. This indicates that the experience of effortful thinking itself—even when devoid of any subject content—improves general cognitive capacity. Finally, we complement these results with quasi-experimental variation indicating that an additional year of schooling improves cognitive endurance, but only in higher-quality schools. Our ﬁndings suggest that schooling disparities may further disadvantage poor children by hampering the development of a core mental capacity.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: within-test performance decline over time (e.g., change in probability correct from early to late questions) on listening-comprehension, Raven’s matrices, and math tests; supplemented by sustained-attention task scores and classroom attentiveness ratings
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: assignment to additional 20-minute sessions of sustained cognitive practice during school day using (i) math-problem practice software or (ii) nonacademic cognitive games, versus status-quo study hall
empirical_analysis.methodology: Individual-level random assignment of primary-school students to cognitive-practice arms or control; estimate impacts on cognitive-fatigue gradients in tests and on school grades in core subjects not directly trained (Hindi/English).
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Stratification and balance checks; alternative constructions of fatigue/decline measures; placebo effects on early-test performance; cross-randomized incentives to separate motivation from endurance; heterogeneity by baseline ability and school characteristics; medium-run persistence checks months after intervention.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Six low-income private primary schools near Lucknow, India; 1,636 students in grades 1–5; intervention during elective/study-hall periods 1–3 times per week from Aug 2018–Jan 2019 with endline testing in spring 2019 plus follow-up measures.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: class-section stratification; baseline math-test score strata; grade fixed effects and school fixed effects in main specifications
subject: Test whether increasing sustained effortful thinking during the school day builds children’s cognitive endurance and improves broader school performance.

metadata.title: CAN POLLUTION MARKETS WORK IN DEVELOPING COUNTRIES? EXPERIMENTAL EVIDENCE FROM INDIA

raw_text.abstract: Market-based environmental regulations are seldom used in low-income countries, where pollution is highest but state capacity is often low. We collaborated with the Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB) to design and experimentally evaluate the world’s ﬁrst particulate-matter emissions market, which covered industrial plants in a large Indian city. There are three main ﬁndings. First, the market functioned well. Treatment plants, randomly assigned to the emissions market, traded permits to become signiﬁcant net sellers or buyers. After trading, treatment plants held enough permits to cover their emissions 99% of the time, compared with just 66% compliance with standards under the command-and-control status quo. Second, treatment plants reduced pollution emissions, relative to control plants, by 20%–30%. Third, the market reduced abatement costs by an estimated 11%, holding constant emissions. This cost-savings estimate is based on plant-speciﬁc marginal cost curves that we estimate from the universe of bids to buy and sell permits in the market. The combination of pollution reductions and low costs imply that the emissions market has mortality beneﬁts that exceed its costs by at least 25 times.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: particulate-matter load (kg) emitted per plant-period constructed from continuous emissions monitoring system (CEMS) readings, aggregated to plant-month/compliance-period totals with specified imputation for missing data
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: indicator for random assignment of industrial plants to participate in the particulate-emissions cap-and-trade program (permit market) versus remaining under command-and-control standards
empirical_analysis.methodology: Field-scale policy experiment allocating plants into an emissions-permit market; estimate treatment effects on emissions and compliance; infer abatement-cost savings using plant-level marginal abatement cost curves estimated from the universe of permit bids.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Alternative missing-data imputations for CEMS nonreporting; specifications excluding COVID shutdown periods and including later periods; checks using baseline balance and alternative pollution measures; sensitivity of cost estimates to alternative MAC functional forms and emissions targets.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Surat, Gujarat (India) particulate emissions market launched 2019; sample of 318 large coal-burning plants mandated to install CEMS, with 162 assigned to market treatment and 156 controls; evaluation spans Sept 2019–Apr 2021 across multiple 4–6 week compliance periods (with COVID interruption).
empirical_analysis.control_variables: baseline plant characteristics (scale, sector, abatement equipment); compliance-period fixed effects; imputation-rule indicators for CEMS data availability
subject: Evaluate whether a cap-and-trade market for particulate emissions can improve compliance, reduce pollution, and lower abatement costs in a low-state-capacity setting.

metadata.title: THE IMPACT OF BEING DENIED A WANTED ABORTION ON WOMEN AND THEIR CHILDREN

raw_text.abstract: This article examines the impact of denying a wanted abortion on women and children in Colombia using high-quality administrative microdata and credibly exogenous variation in abortion access. Women can seek legal abortions through a tutela, with cases randomly assigned to judges. Female judges are 20 percentage points (32%) less likely to deny abortion cases than are male judges, and we use the judge’s sex as an instrument for abortion denial. Denial of a wanted abortion has both immediate and lasting effects. It increases a woman’s risk of death by 2.5 percentage points within nine months, mainly due to unsafe abortion procedures, and raises the likelihood of carrying the pregnancy to term by 31 percentage points. Tracking outcomes up to 15 years later, we ﬁnd that women denied an abortion experience more health issues, lower educational attainment, reduced labor force participation, and higher rates of single motherhood, poverty, and reliance on government assistance. Existing children, born before their mother sought an abortion, are less likely to attend school and are more likely to work.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: indicator for woman’s death within nine months of filing an abortion-rights tutela, measured in national vital statistics death records with cause-of-death coding
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: indicator that the abortion-rights tutela was denied by the randomly assigned judge (first-instance decision), instrumented by judge sex (female vs male) in the random assignment process
empirical_analysis.methodology: Link abortion-rights tutela filings to judge assignment and administrative outcomes; use random assignment of tutelas to judges and judge-sex variation in denial propensity to estimate causal effects of abortion denial on women’s short-run mortality and long-run socioeconomic outcomes, and on outcomes of existing children.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Alternative instruments using judge-specific denial rates (leave-one-out) and judge fixed effects; balance tests for random assignment; placebo tests using outcomes observed before filing; sensitivity to restricting to cases with complete documentation and to office/time controls; robustness across follow-up horizons.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Medellín, Colombia: universe of abortion-rights tutelas filed 2006–2022 linked to national birth and death records (2007–2023) and SISBEN administrative socioeconomic data (SISBEN III/IV), tracking women up to ~15 years after filing and measuring outcomes for pre-existing children.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: filing-time controls; tutela office indicators; claimant baseline demographics and socioeconomic status from SISBEN; case characteristics where available
subject: Estimate the causal impacts of being denied a wanted legal abortion on women’s mortality and long-run socioeconomic outcomes, and on their existing children’s schooling and work.

metadata.title: RACE TO THE BOTTOM: COMPETITION AND QUALITY IN SCIENCE

raw_text.abstract: This article investigates how competition to publish ﬁrst and thereby establish priority affects the quality of scientiﬁc research. We begin by developing a model where scientists decide whether and how long to work on a given project. When deciding how long they should let their projects mature, scientists trade off the marginal beneﬁt of higher-quality research against the marginal risk of being preempted. Projects with the highest scientiﬁc potential are the most competitive because they induce the most entry. Therefore, the model predicts these projects are also the most rushed and lowest quality. We test the predictions of this model in the ﬁeld of structural biology using data from the Protein Data Bank (PDB), a repository for structures of large macromolecules. An important feature of the PDB is that it assigns objective measures of scientiﬁc quality to each structure. As suggested by the model, we ﬁnd that structures with higher ex ante potential generate more competition, are completed faster, and are lower quality. Consistent with the model, and with a causal interpretation of our empirical results, these relationships are mitigated when we focus on structures deposited by scientists who—by nature of their employment position—are less focused on publication and priority. We estimate that the costs associated with improving these low-quality structures are between $1.5 and $8.8 billion since the PDB’s founding in 1971.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: Protein Data Bank (PDB) quality index combining standardized refinement resolution, R-free, and Ramachandran-outlier measures computed/validated by PDB for deposited protein structures
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: priority-race intensity measured by the presence/number of contemporaneous teams solving the same or highly similar protein structure using PDB structure-similarity groupings and timestamped milestones (collection and deposition dates)
empirical_analysis.methodology: Construct ex ante project potential from protein characteristics by predicting future citations, measure competitive entry via simultaneous/near-simultaneous structure discoveries, and relate competition and potential to project maturation time and objective structure-quality metrics in PDB; complement with comparisons to less priority-driven structural genomics deposits and a scientist survey experiment.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Controls for structural complexity and protein characteristics; within-journal and within-protein-family comparisons; split-sample analysis for structural genomics vs non-structural-genomics deposits; alternative competition definitions and time windows; survey-based manipulation checks on perceived competition and effort/quality-control choices.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Protein Data Bank (PDB) near-universe of macromolecular structure deposits since 1971, focusing on X-ray crystallography structures with modern validation metrics and observable project timelines (collection vs deposition dates, especially post-1999).
empirical_analysis.control_variables: protein characteristics (type, organism, gene linkage), project complexity proxies, year and field controls, depositor type (structural genomics vs other) and publication controls
subject: Assess whether competition for scientific priority causes researchers to rush projects and reduce objective research quality in structural biology.

metadata.title: THE EFFECTS OF MEDICAL DEBT RELIEF: EVIDENCE FROM TWO RANDOMIZED EXPERIMENTS

raw_text.abstract: Two in ﬁve Americans have medical debt, nearly half of whom owe at least $2,500. Concerned by this burden, governments and private donors have undertaken large, high-proﬁle efforts to relieve medical debt. We partnered with RIP Medical Debt (now Undue Medical Debt) to conduct two randomized experiments that relieved medical debt with a face value of $169 million for 83,401 people between 2018 and 2020. Our experiments focused on downstream medical debt that had been sold to debt collectors, and one of our experiments straddled an industry-wide pullback in the reporting of medical debt to the credit bureaus, allowing us to estimate the effects of debt relief with and without counterfactual reporting. We track outcomes using credit reports, collections account data, and a multimodal survey. There are three sets of results. First, we ﬁnd a modest improvement in credit access when there is counterfactual credit reporting, but no impact on credit report outcomes when there is not. Second, we estimate that debt relief causes a moderate but statistically signiﬁcant reduction in payments of existing medical bills. Third, we ﬁnd no effects on survey measures of mental and physical health, healthcare utilization, and ﬁnancial wellness. Taken together, our results indicate that the strong correlations documented in prior research do not translate into causal effects for downstream medical debt relief.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: consumer credit score and related credit-bureau outcomes from de-identified TransUnion quarterly credit reports (e.g., delinquencies, credit limits, collections)
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: assignment to medical debt forgiveness via RIP Medical Debt purchases of collection accounts (hospital-debt and collector-debt randomized interventions), including a subexperiment where debts were counterfactually reported to credit bureaus
empirical_analysis.methodology: Two randomized debt-forgiveness experiments with staggered purchase waves; track outcomes in credit reports and supplemental collections-account data; survey a subsample for health, healthcare use, and financial well-being; separately estimate effects under environments with and without counterfactual credit reporting.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Pre-registered outcome families and multiple-testing adjustments; alternative specifications and event-time windows; heterogeneity by baseline collections/debt; robustness to defining treatment at first-wave exposure; separate analysis of the credit-reporting subsample.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: United States, 2018–2020: debt relief with face value $169 million for 83,401 people through two randomized experiments (hospital debt across 18 waves; older collector debt in 2 waves), linked to at least 1 year pre and 1 year post TransUnion credit reports; multimodal survey of 2,888 individuals in the hospital-debt sample.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: randomization strata (debt amount, state, insurance status, collections score) where applicable; wave fixed effects; time fixed effects; baseline credit outcomes
subject: Estimate how forgiving downstream medical debt affects credit outcomes, repayment behavior on other bills, and health and healthcare use.

metadata.title: THE EARNINGS AND LABOR SUPPLY OF U.S. PHYSICIANS

raw_text.abstract: Is government guiding the invisible hand at the top of the labor market? We use new administrative data to measure physicians’ earnings and estimate the inﬂuence of health care policies on these earnings, physicians’ labor supply, and the allocation of talent. Combining the administrative registry of U.S. physicians with tax data, Medicare billing records, and survey responses, we ﬁnd that physicians’ annual earnings average $350,000 and make up 8.6% of national health care spending. Business income makes up one-quarter of earnings and is systematically underreported in survey data. Earnings increase steeply early in the career, and there are major differences across specialties, regions, and ﬁrm sizes. The geographic pattern of earnings is unusual compared with other workers. We argue that these patterns reﬂect policy choices to subsidize demand for physician care, ampliﬁed by restrictions on physician entry, especially in certain specialties.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: physician annual earnings measured as individual total income from IRS tax returns (wage income from W-2 plus business/pass-through income), inflation-adjusted to 2017 dollars
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: policy-driven changes in physician-service payment rates (Medicare Physician Fee Schedule reimbursements) and public-insurance coverage expansions that shift demand for physician services, mapped to physicians via Medicare billing and specialty
empirical_analysis.methodology: Link the universe physician registry to administrative tax data, Medicare billing records, and survey data; document earnings distributions and decompose variation across physicians, locations, specialties, and firm sizes; use reimbursement-rate and coverage-policy variation to estimate pass-through to earnings, procedure supply responses, retirement timing, and specialty-choice reallocations.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Alternative income definitions (AGI vs individual income; wages vs business income); comparisons with survey-reported earnings and with lawyers; sensitivity to specialty and location definitions; robustness across age cohorts and practice-size samples; checks using alternative policy-shock constructions.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: United States physician-year panel 2005–2017 from IRS individual tax returns linked to NPPES physician registry, Medicare billing microdata (post-2012) and Physician Fee Schedule rates, plus restricted-use ACS survey responses and NRMP specialty-match aggregates.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: age and cohort effects; specialty fixed effects; commuting-zone/location fixed effects; firm-size controls; Medicare service-mix controls; time fixed effects
subject: Measure physicians’ earnings and quantify how public insurance and Medicare payment policies shape earnings, labor supply, and specialty talent allocation.

metadata.title: THE DIFFUSION OF NEW TECHNOLOGIES

raw_text.abstract: We identify phrases associated with novel technologies using textual analysis of patents, job postings, and earnings calls, enabling us to identify four stylized facts on the diffusion of jobs relating to new technologies. First, the development of economically impactful new technologies is geographically highly concentrated, more so even than overall patenting: 56% of the most economically impactful technologies come from just two U.S. locations, Silicon Valley and the Northeast Corridor. Second, as the technologies mature and the number of related jobs grows, hiring spreads geographically. This process is very slow, taking around 50 years to disperse fully. Third, while initial hiring in new technologies is highly skill-biased, over time the mean skill level in new positions declines, drawing in an increasing number of lower-skilled workers. Finally, the geographic spread of hiring is slowest for higher-skilled positions, with the locations where new technologies were pioneered remaining the focus for the technology’s high-skill jobs for decades.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: geographic concentration/dispersion of technology-related hiring measured using the coefficient of variation of a technology’s job-posting share across U.S. CBSAs and related concentration metrics from job-posting counts
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: years since a technology’s emergence year, where emergence is defined by the first sustained acceleration in cite-weighted patent mentions for technology phrases identified from patent text and mapped to Wikipedia technology pages
empirical_analysis.methodology: Identify novel-technology phrases from patent text, filter to technologies via Wikipedia pages, date and locate technology origins using patent-inventor addresses, and track technology-related hiring using millions of online job postings and earnings-call mentions; estimate stylized facts on geographic and skill diffusion over time.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Alternative phrase-length choices (unigrams/bigrams/trigrams) and thresholds; human audits of identified technologies; alternative emergence-year and pioneer-location definitions; sensitivity to job-posting text trimming and alternative skill measures.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: U.S. utility patents with application years 1976–2014, Wikipedia technology-page mappings, corporate earnings-call transcripts 2002–2019, and ~200 million online job postings (primarily 2010–2019) geo-coded to 917 CBSAs with occupation-based skill measures from ACS.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: technology fixed effects; year effects; CBSA fixed effects where applicable; occupation/industry controls in job-posting aggregations
subject: Track how new technologies spread across U.S. regions and skill levels by linking patent-based technology emergence to technology-related hiring in job postings.

metadata.title: “SOMETHING WORKS” IN U.S. JAILS: MISCONDUCT AND RECIDIVISM EFFECTS OF THE IGNITE PROGRAM

raw_text.abstract: A long-standing and inﬂuential view in U.S. correctional policy is that “nothing works” when it comes to rehabilitating incarcerated individuals. We revisit this hypothesis by studying an innovative law-enforcement-led program launched in the county jail of Flint, MI: Inmate Growth Naturally and Intentionally through Education (IGNITE). We develop an instrumental variables approach to estimate the effects of IGNITE exposure, leveraging quasi-random court delays that cause individuals to spend more time in jail before and after the program’s launch. Holding time in jail ﬁxed, we ﬁnd that one additional month of IGNITE exposure reduces weekly misconduct in jail by 25% and three-month recidivism by 24%, with the recidivism effects growing over time. Surveys of staff and community members, along with administrative test-score records and within-jail text messages, suggest that cultural change and improved literacy and numeracy scores are contributing mechanisms.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: indicator for rebooking in jail within three months after release (and longer horizons up to one year) using jail management system records from Genesee and Saginaw Counties
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: months of exposure to the IGNITE jail education program, determined by overlap of an individual’s jail spell with the post–September 2020 program period; instrumented by quasi-random court delays that extend time in jail
empirical_analysis.methodology: Use administrative court delays as an instrument for time exposed to IGNITE and difference pre- vs post-launch IV estimates while holding overall jail time fixed; estimate effects on within-jail major misconduct and post-release recidivism and explore mechanisms using education test scores, internal messages, and stakeholder surveys.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Diagnostics for as-good-as-random delay assignment and monotonicity; balance of compliers pre/post; alternative delay measures and court subsets; alternative recidivism definitions (recharge/reconviction); checks for COVID-period confounding and reporting changes; cross-county comparison and double difference specifications.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Genesee County Jail (Flint, Michigan) with IGNITE launched Sept 2020; administrative jail records 2015–2023 linked to district/circuit court registers of action, incident reports on misconduct, internal messaging logs, and standardized literacy/numeracy test scores from the partner education provider; supplemented by community and staff surveys collected 2023–2024.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: time-in-jail measures; charge and court indicators; calendar-time effects; demographic controls (age, race, sex) and prior criminal-history proxies
subject: Estimate whether exposure to a jail-based education and culture-change program reduces in-jail misconduct and post-release recidivism.

metadata.title: Teacher Labor Market Policy and the Theory of the Second Best

raw_text.abstract: We estimate a matching model of teachers and elementary schools with rich data on teachers’ applications and principals’ ratings from a large, urban district in North Carolina. Both teachers’ and principals’ preferences deviate from those that would maximize the achievement of economically disadvantaged students: teachers prefer schools with fewer disadvantaged students, and principals’ ratings are weakly related to teacher effectiveness. In equilibrium, these two deviations combine to produce a surprisingly equitable current allocation, where teacher quality is balanced across advantaged and disadvantaged students. To close achievement gaps, policies that address deviations on one side alone are ineffective or harmful, while policies that address both could substantially increase the achievement of disadvantaged students. JEL codes: I24, J23, J45.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: teacher value-added to student math achievement estimated from linked student standardized test-score gains (with specifications allowing differential effects by disadvantaged vs advantaged students)
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: school/classroom share (or count) of economically disadvantaged students based on federal program eligibility in administrative records
empirical_analysis.methodology: Estimate teacher value-added from student test scores; recover teacher preferences from observed job applications and principals’ preferences from application ratings; estimate a two-sided teacher–school matching equilibrium and simulate policy counterfactuals (teacher bonuses for disadvantaged schools and principal hiring rules based on effectiveness).
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Alternative value-added models (homogeneous vs heterogeneous); include novice teachers via residual-based measures or imputation; re-estimate preferences under alternative choice-set constructions and vacancy-timing restrictions; equilibrium simulations under alternative market-clearing timing.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Large urban school district in North Carolina: teacher vacancy postings and 346,663 applications (2010–2019) linked to state administrative teacher records and student test scores (NCERDC) for elementary grades.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: teacher experience/credentials, commute time, school demographics and baseline achievement, grade/year effects, and other teacher and school observables used in value-added and preference models
subject: Quantify how teacher and principal preferences shape the allocation of effective teachers across disadvantaged and advantaged elementary schools and evaluate which policies can close achievement gaps.

metadata.title: Putting Quantitative Models to the Test: An Application to the U.S.-China Trade War

raw_text.abstract: The primary motivation behind quantitative work in international trade and many other fields is to shed light on the economic consequences of policy changes and other shocks. To help assess and potentially strengthen the credibility of such quantitative predictions, we introduce an IV-based goodness-of-fit measure that provides the basis for testing causal predictions in arbitrary general equilibrium environments as well as for estimating the average misspecification in these predictions. As an illustration of how to use the measure in practice, we revisit the welfare consequences of the U.S.-China trade war predicted by Fajgelbaum et al. (2020). JEL codes: C01, F10.

theoretical_summary: Develops an IV-based goodness-of-fit measure to test the causal predictions of quantitative general-equilibrium models and illustrates the approach by evaluating welfare predictions for the U.S.–China trade war.

metadata.title: Officer-Involved: The Media Language of Police Killings

raw_text.abstract: This article examines language patterns in U.S. television news coverage of police killings. First, we document that the media use syntactic structures—such as passive voice, nominalizations, and intransitive verbs—that obscure responsibility more often in cases of police killings than in cases of civilian killings. Through an online experiment, we demonstrate the significance of these syntactic differences, revealing that participants are less likely to hold police officers morally responsible and demand penalties when exposed to obfuscatory language, particularly in cases involving unarmed victims. Further analysis of news data shows greater use of obfuscatory language when the victims are unarmed or video footage is available—situations in which obfuscation may have the greatest impact. Exploring the causes of this differential obfuscation, we do not find evidence that it is driven by either demand-side factors or supply-side factors associated with TV station ownership and political leaning. Instead, our results suggest that narratives crafted by police departments are more likely drivers of media obfuscation. This article highlights how syntactic choices and their semantic consequences in media shape perceptions, extending beyond coverage volume and bias. JEL codes: K14, K42, L82.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: sentence-level indicator for obfuscatory syntax in closed-caption transcripts (passive voice, nominalizations such as “officer-involved shooting,” omission of agent, or intransitive constructions) identified via semantic-role labeling and coreference resolution
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: incident type indicator: news stories matched to police killings (Mapping Police Violence) versus civilian gun homicides with identified suspects (Gun Violence Archive)
empirical_analysis.methodology: Match killings to TV news stories and extract sentences describing the incident; measure syntactic obfuscation and compare police-killing vs civilian-homicide coverage; complement with an online experiment that randomizes sentence structures to test effects on perceived officer responsibility, penalties, and support for reform.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Station/media-market fixed effects; analyses restricted to first sentence of a story; alternative story-matching thresholds; excluding sentences with suspect names; heterogeneity by unarmed status, video availability, and fleeing status.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Universe of U.S. local and national TV news closed captions (2013–2019) matched to police killings (MPV, 2013–2019) and civilian gun homicides (GVA, 2014–2018); online experiment on Prolific (March 2022).
empirical_analysis.control_variables: victim demographics (age, gender, race), incident context (unarmed, body-camera video), time and station/market controls, and story-position controls (e.g., first sentence)
subject: Measure whether and when television news uses language that obscures responsibility in police killings, and assess how such language shapes public perceptions of accountability.

metadata.title: Exploitation through Racialization

raw_text.abstract: I develop a model of the social construction of race. Racial categories emerge from labor conflict when elites privilege intrinsically irrelevant traits to divide workers against each other and extract workers’ surplus. I show that elites use color to grant unequal rights and track these rights across generations because it is heritable, observable, and relatively immutable. Depending on the demographic conditions the elites face, the system of racialization manifests either as ancestry-based or color-based categories. This approach to the social construction of race provides a unified explanation of skin-tone inequality, racial homophily in marriage, the social status of mixed-race people, the psychological wage of Jim Crow, and legal restrictions on manumission. I test for historical variations in racial boundaries using census data from the United States and Brazil and for differential patterns of skin-tone inequality between ancestry-based and color-based systems using survey data from across the Americas. JEL codes: D74, F54, P48, Z13.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: years of schooling / educational attainment from harmonized survey microdata across the Americas (with comparable analyses for income outcomes)
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: skin-tone measure from survey instruments (e.g., ordered scale with multiple categories) coded so higher values indicate darker skin
empirical_analysis.methodology: Develop a political-economy model of racialization as an elite divide-and-rule strategy and test its predictions using historical census data (U.S. and Brazil) and cross-country survey microdata; compare how skin-tone gradients and mixed-race status vary between ancestry-based and color-based racial systems tied to demographic conditions during slavery.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Alternative system classifications and sample restrictions; controls for region/cohort composition; sensitivity to different skin-tone coding and outcome definitions; within-country comparisons across regions with different slavery-era demographics.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Historical censuses (Brazil 1872; U.S. 1800 and 1880 linked at county level) plus survey microdata for 26 countries across the Americas with skin-tone measures and socioeconomic outcomes.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: age, sex, location fixed effects, socioeconomic baseline controls, and race-category indicators where applicable; regional slavery-era demographic measures in historical tests
subject: Explain how slavery-era elite strategies created racial categories and quantify how skin tone and racial system type relate to long-run socioeconomic inequality.

metadata.title: Wage Hysteresis and Entitlement Effects: The Persistent Impacts of a Temporary Overtime Policy

raw_text.abstract: This article studies the unexpected retraction of a U.S. federal policy in 2016 that would have more than doubled the “overtime exemption threshold” from $455 to $913 per week and thereby grant overtime protection to an additional 20% of salaried workers. Although the policy was blocked by a federal court injunction a week before it was supposed to take effect, I show that it nevertheless had a persistent positive impact on workers’ earnings. Leveraging a bunching design with administrative payroll data from ADP, I find that employers raised workers’ salaries to the $913 threshold even after the policy was repealed. Over the next 18 months, difference-in-difference estimates reveal that employers did not slow the wage growth of workers affected by the policy relative to those already earning above $913 per week, nor did they hire new employees at a lower pay rate. Real wages remained persistently elevated relative to what they would have been absent the policy and separation rates decreased among workers bunched at the $913 threshold. Comparing highly exposed firms to unaffected firms, I find an increase in employers’ wage bills but no change in aggregate employment. Taken together, the results indicate that temporary policies impacting wage levels can have permanent effects on the labor market. Survey responses collected by the Department of Labor suggest that morale concerns play a key role in driving the wage hysteresis. JEL codes: D63, E64, J31, J38, J30, J80, D22, D90.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: weekly base pay for salaried workers constructed from ADP administrative payroll records (salary per pay period converted to weekly base pay per FLSA rules)
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: exposure to the proposed $913/week overtime exemption threshold based on pre-policy weekly base pay relative to $455–$913; treatment intensity captured by bunching at $913 and firm exposure (baseline share below $913)
empirical_analysis.methodology: Use the 2016 announced-but-enjoined federal overtime threshold increase as a natural experiment; estimate bunching at $913 using pre-period distributions as counterfactuals; estimate wage-growth, new-hire, separation, and firm-level effects with difference-in-differences comparisons to workers/firms above the threshold.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Placebo comparisons using earlier years; alternative bin widths and counterfactual distributions; tests around legal-information milestones (injunction and final decision); sensitivity to restricting to continuously operating firms and alternative outcome windows.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: U.S. ADP monthly payroll microdata (May 2008–Jan 2020), focusing on salaried workers around the 2016 overtime-rule episode and tracking outcomes for at least 18 months after the injunction; supplemented with U.S. Department of Labor employer survey responses.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: time fixed effects, firm fixed effects (where applicable), baseline pay level and pay-frequency controls, industry/state controls, and firm exposure measures
subject: Test whether a rescinded overtime-rule salary threshold created persistent wage increases through entitlement and morale-based wage rigidity.

metadata.title: Manufacturing Revolutions: Industrial Policy and Industrialization in South Korea

raw_text.abstract: I study the effect of industrial policies on industrial development by considering an important episode during the East Asian miracle: South Korea’s heavy and chemical industry (HCI) drive, 1973–1979. Based on newly assembled data, I use the introduction and termination of industrial policies to study their effects during and after the intervention period. I show that HCI policies promoted the expansion and dynamic comparative advantage of directly targeted industries and indirectly benefited downstream users through input–output linkages, with effects that persisted after the policy ended and in some cases materialized with lags. JEL codes: L5, O14, O25, N6.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: log real gross output shipped by manufacturing industry from Korea’s Mining and Manufacturing Surveys/Census (MMS), harmonized across KSIC code revisions
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: indicator that an industry is designated as a Heavy and Chemical Industry (HCI) target in major policy acts (steel, nonferrous metals, shipbuilding, machinery, electronics, petrochemicals) plus input–output–based exposure measures to targeted intermediates
empirical_analysis.methodology: Estimate dynamic sector-level responses to the 1973–1979 HCI drive by comparing targeted and non-targeted manufacturing industries before, during, and after the policy period; quantify downstream spillovers using input–output linkage exposure; validate with cross-country comparisons and additional productivity evidence.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Double-robust reweighting of controls using propensity scores; cross-country triple-difference placebo comparisons; alternative treatment coding and pre-trend tests; sensitivity to adding pre-1973 industry controls and using alternative comparative-advantage measures.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: South Korea 1967–1986: newly assembled industry panels from EPB MMS surveys/censuses, digitized 1970 input–output tables, producer price indices, and trade-flow data (UN Comtrade) with trade-policy measures for selected years.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: industry and year fixed effects; pre-1973 industry averages (material costs, wage bill per worker, plant size, baseline productivity); trade-policy controls and linkage controls in spillover analyses
subject: Estimate whether South Korea’s 1973–1979 heavy-industry industrial policy shifted manufacturing output and comparative advantage and generated spillovers through input–output linkages.

metadata.title: Systemic Discrimination: Theory and Measurement

raw_text.abstract: Economists often measure discrimination as disparities arising from the direct effects of group identity. We develop new tools to model and measure systemic discrimination, capturing how discrimination in other decisions indirectly contributes to disparities. A novel experimental design, the iterated audit, identifies systemic discrimination. We illustrate these new tools in two field experiments. The first experiment shows how racial discrimination can accumulate across multiple rounds of hiring through the interaction of two forces: greater discrimination against inexperienced workers, which affects the opportunity to obtain experience, and high subsequent returns to experience. The second experiment shows how gender-based differences in the language of recommendation letters can translate into systemic gender discrimination in STEM hiring. We discuss how our findings qualify previous results on direct discrimination and how our tools can be used to target policy interventions. JEL codes: D63, D83, J16, J71.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: employer callback / evaluation outcomes elicited from hiring decisions on fictitious applications, including differences by applicant group and by experience or recommendation-letter content
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: resume attribute indicating prior work experience (or simulated experience accumulation across rounds) and related signal content embedded in application materials
empirical_analysis.methodology: Develop a system-based framework that decomposes hiring disparities into direct and systemic components; implement an iterated-audit design across decision nodes and illustrate it with two studies: (i) how unequal access to early experience and high returns to experience compound racial hiring disparities, and (ii) how gendered recommendation-letter language translates into downstream STEM hiring disparities.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Randomization and balance checks within experimental arms; sensitivity to alternative assumptions mapping callbacks to offers/experience; heterogeneity analyses by baseline experience; alternative constructions of recommendation-letter language and evaluator decision thresholds.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Two field experiments in labor-market hiring settings (early-2020s): a multi-round hiring audit varying race and experience and a lab-in-the-field evaluation of STEM application packets differing only in gendered recommendation-letter language.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: job and location controls in hiring studies; applicant skill proxies held fixed by construction (resume templates); evaluator fixed effects where applicable
subject: Provide a framework and evidence for how discrimination in earlier decisions accumulates into systemic discrimination in later hiring outcomes.

metadata.title: Structural Estimation under Misspecification: Theory and Implications for Practice

raw_text.abstract: A researcher can use a tightly parameterized structural model to obtain internally consistent estimates of a wide range of economically interesting targets. We ask how reliable these estimates are when the researcher’s model may be misspecified. We focus on the case of multivariate, potentially nonlinear models where the causal variable of interest is endogenous. Reliable estimates require that the researcher’s model is flexible enough to describe the effects of the endogenous variable approximately correctly. Reliable estimates do not require that the researcher has correctly specified the role of the exogenous controls in the model. However, if the role of the controls is misspecified, reliable estimates require a property we call strong exclusion. Strong exclusion depends on having sufficiently many instruments that are unrelated to the controls. We discuss how practitioners can achieve strong exclusion, and illustrate our findings with an application to a differentiated goods model of demand for beer. JEL codes: C36, L13, D24.

theoretical_summary: Analyzes when IV-based structural estimators remain approximately causally reliable under model misspecification and shows that achieving this robustness hinges on a ‘strong exclusion’ condition, illustrated in a differentiated-goods demand application.

metadata.title: The Race between Education, Technology, and the Minimum Wage

raw_text.abstract: What is the effect of the real minimum wage on wages and inequality? I develop a theory that nests the race between education and technology. The theory predicts that the effect of changes in minimum wages is initially small but grows over time. I present empirical evidence of these dynamic effects: the elasticity of real wages grows substantially over a three-year period. I show that minimum wages help rationalize a considerable decline in real wages of low-education workers in the 1980s and play a role in shaping the evolution of the U.S. college premium. JEL codes: J0, J2, J3, J4.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: composition-adjusted real wages (and the college wage premium) computed from CPS microdata and deflated price indices, aggregated by worker group and state over multi-year horizons
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: real minimum wage measured as the employment-weighted average of state statutory minimum wages (max of state and federal) deflated by the GDP deflator; treatment intensity captured by each group’s minimum-wage bite
empirical_analysis.methodology: Develop a dynamic job-ladder model combining education supply, technology demand, and minimum-wage wage-setting frictions; estimate dynamic effects using distributed-lag specifications that interact lagged minimum-wage changes with group-by-state minimum-wage bite and aggregate time-series evidence on the college premium.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Alternative time-trend specifications and sample windows; heterogeneity by education/age groups; alternative minimum-wage series (federal vs state-weighted); sensitivity to measurement-error corrections in minimum-wage bite and additional controls for expected policy changes.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: United States: CPS microdata covering earnings years 1963–2016 for national time-series estimates and a state-by-worker-group panel (50 states × 100 demographic/education groups) over half-year periods 1979–2016 for dynamic wage responses; state minimum-wage law histories.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: relative supply measures by education group, flexible time trends, state and group fixed effects, and controls for expected minimum-wage exposure based on pre-period bite
subject: Quantify the dynamic impact of real minimum wages on real wages and inequality within a framework that nests the race between education and technology.
